claim: Tumors are composed of many different cell types including cancer cells, fibroblasts, and immune cells.
source: Tumors are composed of many different cell types including cancer cells, fibroblasts, and immune cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about tumor composition.

claim: Dissecting functional metabolic differences between cell types within a mixed population can be challenging due to the rapid turnover of metabolites relative to the time needed to isolate cells.
source: Dissecting functional metabolic differences between cell types within a mixed population can be challenging due to the rapid turnover of metabolites relative to the time needed to isolate cells.
evidence: This is a statement about technical challenges in the field, supported by established knowledge about metabolite turnover rates.

claim: Isotope-labeled nutrients can be traced into macromolecules that turn over more slowly than metabolites.
source: To overcome this challenge, we traced isotope-labeled nutrients into macromolecules that turn over more slowly than metabolites.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study, supported by the experimental design.

claim: Pancreatic cancer cells exhibited increased pyruvate carboxylation relative to fibroblasts in murine pancreatic cancer organoid-fibroblast co-cultures and tumors.
source: Pancreatic cancer cells exhibited increased pyruvate carboxylation relative to fibroblasts, and this flux depended on both pyruvate carboxylase and malic enzyme 1 activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from organoid co-cultures and tumor experiments.

claim: Pyruvate carboxylation flux in pancreatic cancer cells depended on both pyruvate carboxylase and malic enzyme 1 activity.
source: Pancreatic cancer cells exhibited increased pyruvate carboxylation relative to fibroblasts, and this flux depended on both pyruvate carboxylase and malic enzyme 1 activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genetic manipulation experiments showing effects of PC and ME1 deletion.

claim: Expression of both pyruvate carboxylase and malic enzyme 1 in cancer cells was necessary for organoid and tumor growth.
source: Consequently, expression of both enzymes in cancer cells was necessary for organoid and tumor growth, demonstrating that dissecting the metabolism of specific cell populations within heterogeneous systems can identify dependencies that may not be evident from studying isolated cells in culture or bulk tissue.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing reduced growth upon enzyme deletion.

claim: Environmental context plays an important role in determining how cancer cells use nutrients to proliferate and survive.
source: Environmental context plays an important role in determining how cancer cells use nutrients to proliferate and survive, and non-cancer cells within a tissue can alter nutrient availability (Lyssiotis and Kimmelman, 2017; Mayers and Vander Heiden, 2017; Muir et al., 2018; Pavlova and Thompson, 2016; Sullivan and Vander Heiden, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Non-cancer cells within a tissue can alter nutrient availability.
source: Environmental context plays an important role in determining how cancer cells use nutrients to proliferate and survive, and non-cancer cells within a tissue can alter nutrient availability (Lyssiotis and Kimmelman, 2017; Mayers and Vander Heiden, 2017; Muir et al., 2018; Pavlova and Thompson, 2016; Sullivan and Vander Heiden, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Different cell populations within tumors can compete for limiting nutrients.
source: There is evidence that different cell populations within tumors can compete for limiting nutrients (Chang et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2015; Zecchin et al., 2017), and metabolic cooperation between different cell types can also influence tumor phenotypes (Linares et al., 2017; Sousa et al., 2016; Valencia et al., 2014; Vander Heiden and DeBerardinis, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Metabolic cooperation between different cell types can influence tumor phenotypes.
source: There is evidence that different cell populations within tumors can compete for limiting nutrients (Chang et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2015; Zecchin et al., 2017), and metabolic cooperation between different cell types can also influence tumor phenotypes (Linares et al., 2017; Sousa et al., 2016; Valencia et al., 2014; Vander Heiden and DeBerardinis, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cancer cell metabolism in culture can differ from the metabolism of tumors in vivo.
source: Cancer cell metabolism in culture can differ from the metabolism of tumors in vivo (Biancur et al., 2017; Cantor et al., 2017; Davidson et al., 2016; Mayers and Vander Heiden, 2015; Muir et al., 2017; Sellers et al., 2019; Vande Voorde et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Cancer cells are a minority cell type in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) tumors.
source: For instance, cancer cells are a minority cell type in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) tumors (Feig et al., 2012), and an understanding of cell metabolism in these tumors requires de-convolution of cancer-specific and stroma-specific phenotypes.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The metabolism of cancer cells and different stromal cells isolated from PDAC tumors can be different from each other when studied in culture.
source: Furthermore, there is evidence that the metabolism of cancer cells and different stromal cells isolated from these tumors can be different from each other when studied in culture (Francescone et al., 2018; Halbrook et al., 2019; Sousa et al., 2016), and it is unknown whether the metabolic programs used by different cell populations in culture are also used within PDAC tumors in vivo where environmental conditions are different.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Studies of bulk tumor metabolism fail to capture information about metabolic heterogeneity with regard to different cell types.
source: Studies of bulk tumor metabolism fail to capture information about metabolic heterogeneity with regard to different cell types (Xiao et al., 2019), and existing approaches are limited in their ability to study functional metabolic phenotypes in different cell populations in intact tissue.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Metabolic reactions take place on time scales that are faster than the turnover of many metabolic intermediates.
source: A major limitation arises from the fact that metabolic reactions take place on time scales that are faster than the turnover of many metabolic intermediates, complicating metabolite analysis after tumor digestion and cell sorting (Shamir et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Cell sorting can induce mechanical and oxidative stress and reduce the levels of certain metabolites.
source: For example, sorting can induce mechanical and oxidative stress and reduce the levels of certain metabolites (Binek et al., 2019; Llufrio et al., 2018; Roci et al., 2016), and even adding small amounts of bovine serum to the sorting buffer was not sufficient to prevent changes in some metabolite levels during cell sorting (Llufrio et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Isotopic metabolite labeling patterns can be more robust than metabolite levels when assessing metabolites from flow cytometry sorted cells.
source: Indeed, isotopic metabolite labeling patterns can be more robust than metabolite levels when assessing metabolites from flow cytometry sorted cells, although labeling can also be affected by cell sorting (Roci et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Interpretation of metabolite labeling patterns is influenced by whether cells are at metabolic steady state.
source: Nevertheless, interpretation of metabolite labeling patterns is influenced by whether cells are at metabolic steady state (Buescher et al., 2015), which when coupled with the rapid timescales of metabolism relative to the time needed to isolate cells suggests that new approaches are needed to better understand metabolism of individual cell types within mixed cell populations such as tumors.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: End-product biomass labeling has been applied in studies of microbial metabolism and metabolic engineering to better understand mixed populations of bacteria.
source: This technique has been applied in studies of microbial metabolism and metabolic engineering to better understand mixed populations of bacteria (Gebreselassie and Antoniewicz, 2015; Ghosh et al., 2014; Rühl et al., 2011; Zamboni et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Turnover of end-product macromolecules such as protein is slow relative to the time period needed to isolate tumor cell populations.
source: Unlike short-lived metabolic intermediates, turnover of end-product macromolecules such as protein is slow relative to the time period needed to isolate tumor cell populations.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about protein turnover rates.

claim: Extensive labeling of multiple metabolic intermediates is observed from U-13C-glucose in pancreatic tumors and normal pancreas.
source: Similar to what has been observed with other mouse cancer models and in humans (Davidson et al., 2016; Fan et al., 2009; Hensley et al., 2016; Sellers et al., 2015), extensive labeling of multiple metabolic intermediates is observed from U-13C-glucose in pancreatic tumors and normal pancreas (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3, Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and by citations to prior literature.

claim: Plasma glucose levels were not changed over the course of the U-13C-glucose infusion experiment.
source: To assess U-13C-glucose labeling of metabolites in autochthonous pancreatic tumors arising in the LSL-KrasG12D; Trp53fl/fl; Pdx1-Cre (KP-/-C) (Bardeesy et al., 2006) and the LSL-KrasG12D; Trp53R172H/+; Pdx1-Cre (KPC) (Hingorani et al., 2005) mouse models, we first confirmed that plasma glucose levels were not changed over the course of the experiment (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Enrichment of 13C-glucose in plasma was around 40% in non-tumor-bearing mice, and in both KP-/-C and KPC animals at a glucose infusion rate of 0.4 mg/min.
source: At this rate of glucose infusion, enrichment of 13C-glucose in plasma was around 40% in non-tumor-bearing mice, and in both KP-/-C and KPC animals (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Labeling of pyruvate, lactate, alanine, and serine from U-13C-glucose was observed in normal pancreas tissue and in tumors arising in both KP-/-C and KPC models.
source: Under these conditions, labeling of pyruvate and lactate, as well as the glucose-derived amino acids alanine and serine, from U-13C-glucose was observed in normal pancreas tissue and in tumors arising in both models (Figure 1C–F, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-F.

claim: Labeling of TCA cycle metabolites was observed in normal pancreas tissue and in PDAC tumors from both KP-/-C and KPC models.
source: Labeling of TCA cycle metabolites was also observed in normal pancreas tissue and in PDAC tumors from both models (Figure 1G–L, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-L.

claim: PDH decarboxylates three-carbon pyruvate to two-carbon acetyl-CoA, resulting in an M+2 labeling pattern in TCA cycle metabolites when 13C-labeled pyruvate is metabolized via PDH.
source: PDH decarboxylates three-carbon pyruvate to two-carbon acetyl-CoA, and therefore if 13C-labeled pyruvate is metabolized via PDH, a two carbon (M+2) labeling pattern is observed in TCA cycle metabolites as well as in the amino acid aspartate (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on established biochemical knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1G.

claim: PC carboxylates three-carbon pyruvate to four-carbon oxaloacetate, resulting in an M+3 labeling pattern when unlabeled CO2 is added to 13C-labeled pyruvate via this enzyme.
source: In contrast, PC carboxylates three-carbon pyruvate to four-carbon oxaloacetate, and therefore if unlabeled CO2 is added to 13C-labeled pyruvate via this enzyme, a three carbon (M+3) labeling pattern is observed (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on established biochemical knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1G.

claim: An increase in both M+2 and M+3 labeling of TCA cycle metabolites and the TCA cycle-derived amino acids aspartate and glutamate was observed in KP-/-C tumor tissue compared to normal pancreas.
source: We observed an increase in both M+2 and M+3 labeling of TCA cycle metabolites and the TCA cycle-derived amino acids aspartate and glutamate in KP-/-C tumor tissue compared to normal pancreas (Figure 1H–N).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H-N.

claim: Cancer cells cannot take up extracellular aspartate in PDAC tumors.
source: Importantly, despite some aspartate labeling in the plasma of infused mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1), prior studies of this model have shown that cancer cells cannot take up extracellular aspartate (Sullivan et al., 2018), arguing that labeled aspartate in plasma contributes minimally to aspartate labeling in cancer cells in PDAC tumors.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Proline was not extensively labeled from glucose in pancreas or PDAC tumor tissue from either KP-/-C or KPC model.
source: Proline was not extensively labeled from glucose in pancreas or PDAC tumor tissue from either model, suggesting that glucose carbon contributes minimally to the synthesis of this amino acid (Figure 1O, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1O.

claim: In KPC mouse PDAC tumors, higher M+2 labeling of only some TCA cycle metabolites compared to normal pancreas was observed, and no increase in M+3 metabolite labeling compared to pancreas was observed.
source: Of note, in KPC mouse PDAC tumors, we observed higher M+2 labeling of only some TCA cycle metabolites compared to normal pancreas, and did not observe an increase in M+3 metabolite labeling compared to pancreas (Figure 1H–O), illustrating that glucose labels metabolites differently in bulk tumors arising in each model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H-O.

claim: Glucose contributes to labeling of TCA cycle carbon via reactions that involve PDH and PC in PDAC tumors.
source: These data suggest that glucose contributes to labeling of TCA cycle carbon via reactions that involve PDH and PC in PDAC tumors, although the extent of labeling depends on the PDAC model used.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing M+2 and M+3 labeling patterns.

claim: Plasma glucose levels were increased as a result of a higher glucose infusion rate (30 mg/kg/min).
source: Plasma glucose levels were increased as a result of this higher infusion rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), and resulted in extensive labeling of glycolytic metabolites and glucose-derived amino acids (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1), as well as an increase in M+2 and M+3 labeling of TCA cycle intermediates and related amino acids in pancreatic tumor tissue relative to normal pancreas (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–N, Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: An increase in M+2 and M+3 labeling of TCA metabolites and aspartate was observed in orthotopic tumor model compared to adjacent normal pancreas.
source: When compared to adjacent normal pancreas, we observed an increase in M+2 and M+3 labeling of TCA metabolites and aspartate in this orthotopic tumor model (Figure 1—figure supplement 3L–O, Figure 1—figure supplement 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3L-O.

claim: Tumors arising from orthotopic transplantation of murine PDAC cells still contain stroma.
source: Regardless, tumors arising from orthotopic transplantation of murine PDAC cells still contain stroma (Danai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Cancer cells are a minority cell population in both autochthonous PDAC tumor models.
source: Thus, tumors in all models considered consist of multiple cell types, and cancer cells are known to be a minority cell population in both autochthonous PDAC tumor models.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about PDAC tumor composition.

claim: Metabolite labeling in tumors will reflect a weighted average of labeling in all cell types present in the tissue sample.
source: In all cases, metabolite labeling will reflect a weighted average of labeling in all cell types present in the tissue sample and this heterogeneity in cell types in all tissues is a limitation to the use of labeled nutrient infusions to understand the metabolism of cancer cells, or any individual cell population, in tumors or other tissues.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the interpretation of bulk tissue labeling data.

claim: Immunohistochemistry analysis of tumors arising in KP-/-C mice revealed higher PC expression in cancer cells.
source: Indeed, immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis of tumors arising in KP-/-C mice revealed higher PC expression in cancer cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Human pancreatic tumors exhibit a range of PC expression levels.
source: Analysis of a human pancreatic tumor tissue by IHC shows that human tumors exhibit a range of PC expression levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D), although higher PC expression is observed in cancer cells compared to stroma (Figure 2B), similar to findings in human lung tumors (Sellers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-D and Figure 2B, and by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Higher PC expression is observed in cancer cells compared to stroma in human pancreatic tumors.
source: Analysis of a human pancreatic tumor tissue by IHC shows that human tumors exhibit a range of PC expression levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D), although higher PC expression is observed in cancer cells compared to stroma (Figure 2B), similar to findings in human lung tumors (Sellers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and by a citation to prior literature.

claim: qPCR analysis of mRNA isolated from sorted cell populations derived from KP-/-C tumors trended toward higher PC expression in cancer cells relative to fibroblasts, although PC mRNA was detected in fibroblasts.
source: However, while IHC can be useful to determine relative expression in tumor sections, it does not prove lack of expression by non-cancer cells. Indeed, qPCR analysis of mRNA isolated from sorted cell populations derived from KP-/-C tumors trended toward higher PC expression in cancer cells relative to fibroblasts, although PC mRNA was detected in fibroblasts (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Metabolic fluxes can be more dependent on metabolite concentrations than enzyme expression levels.
source: Furthermore, metabolic fluxes can be more dependent on metabolite concentrations than enzyme expression levels (Hackett et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: When PDAC cells or PSCs alone are cultured in the presence of 13C-glucose in vitro, PSCs exhibit similar or higher M+3 TCA cycle metabolite labeling than cancer cells.
source: When PDAC cells or PSCs alone are cultured in the presence of 13C-glucose in vitro, PSCs exhibit similar or higher M+3 TCA cycle metabolite labeling than cancer cells (Figure 2D–E), even though the fibroblast cell population exhibited lower PC expression in tumors (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Pancreatic cancer organoid growth becomes dependent on including PSCs in the culture system when exposed to a more minimal medium.
source: To do this, we generated pancreatic cancer organoid cultures from KP-/-C and KPC tumors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; Boj et al., 2015), and found that when exposed to a more minimal medium than is commonly used (Boj et al., 2015), pancreatic cancer organoid growth becomes dependent on including PSCs in the culture system (Figure 2F–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F-G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: When sorted from organoid co-culture system, both cancer cells and PSCs expressed higher levels of PC mRNA compared to PSCs and pancreatic cancer cells in standard monoculture.
source: Relevant to the M+3 labeling of TCA cycle-associated metabolites from glucose observed in pancreatic tumors, when sorted from this co-culture organoid system, both cancer cells and PSCs expressed higher levels of PC mRNA compared to PSCs and pancreatic cancer cells in standard monoculture (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: M+3 labeling of aspartate and malate was observed when U-13C-glucose is provided to whole organoid co-cultures comprised of both cancer cells and PSCs.
source: In addition, when U-13C-glucose is provided to whole organoid co-cultures comprised of both cancer cells and PSCs, and TCA cycle intermediate labeling is assessed after rapid quenching and extraction of metabolites, M+3 labeling of aspartate and malate was observed (Figure 2I–J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–K, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I-J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H-K.

claim: The levels and/or labeling from U-13C-glucose of many metabolites changed over the time required to separate cells using antibodies and/or flow cytometry.
source: Consistent with the known rapid turnover of metabolites (Shamir et al., 2016), the levels (Figure 3A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C, Figure 3—source data 1) and/or labeling from U-13C-glucose (Figure 3E–H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F, Figure 3—source data 1), of many metabolites changed over the time required to separate cells using antibodies and/or flow cytometry.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-F, and by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Glucose labeling of protein was stable over the time period needed to sort cells by flow cytometry.
source: We confirmed that glucose labeling of protein was stable over the time period needed to sort cells by flow cytometry (Figure 3I–J, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I-J.

claim: Amino acids from protein hydrolysates were detectable in sorted cells from murine PDAC tumors, and were within the linear range of detection by GC-MS even when low cell numbers of less abundant cell populations were recovered from tumors.
source: We also confirmed that amino acids from protein hydrolysates were detectable in sorted cells from murine PDAC tumors, and were within the linear range of detection by GC-MS even when low cell numbers of less abundant cell populations were recovered from tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G-L.

claim: tdTomato fluorescence in tumors arising in KP-/-C mice bearing a LSL-tdTomato allele did not co-localize with staining for the fibroblast-specific marker alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA).
source: To investigate whether PDAC cancer cells also exhibit higher pyruvate carboxylation activity in tumors in vivo, we first verified that the tdTomato fluorescence in tumors arising in KP-/-C mice bearing a LSL-tdTomato allele did not co-localize with staining for the fibroblast-specific marker alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) (Figure 5A), but did co-localize with Cytokeratin 19 (CK19), a marker of pancreatic cancer cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: tdTomato fluorescence in tumors arising in KP-/-C mice bearing a LSL-tdTomato allele co-localized with Cytokeratin 19 (CK19), a marker of pancreatic cancer cells.
source: To investigate whether PDAC cancer cells also exhibit higher pyruvate carboxylation activity in tumors in vivo, we first verified that the tdTomato fluorescence in tumors arising in KP-/-C mice bearing a LSL-tdTomato allele did not co-localize with staining for the fibroblast-specific marker alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) (Figure 5A), but did co-localize with Cytokeratin 19 (CK19), a marker of pancreatic cancer cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Over time, similar M+2 protein aspartate labeling was observed between cancer cells and PSCs in organoid co-cultures.
source: Over time, similar M+2 protein aspartate labeling was observed between the two cell types, while higher M+3 aspartate labeling was observed in cancer cells as compared to PSCs, suggesting that while the two cell types have similar labeling via reactions involving PDH, the cancer cells appear to have higher pyruvate carboxylation activity (Figure 4B–C, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Higher M+3 aspartate labeling was observed in cancer cells as compared to PSCs in organoid co-cultures, suggesting that cancer cells have higher pyruvate carboxylation activity.
source: Over time, similar M+2 protein aspartate labeling was observed between the two cell types, while higher M+3 aspartate labeling was observed in cancer cells as compared to PSCs, suggesting that while the two cell types have similar labeling via reactions involving PDH, the cancer cells appear to have higher pyruvate carboxylation activity (Figure 4B–C, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-C and represents an inference from the labeling patterns.

claim: Higher M+3 labeling of glutamate and proline from glucose was observed in cancer cells compared to PSCs in organoid co-cultures.
source: This higher M+3 level was also reflected in the other TCA cycle-derived amino acids glutamate and proline (Figure 4D–G, Figure 4—source data 1), whereas labeling of the glucose-derived amino acids alanine and serine was not higher in cancer cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-G.

claim: Labeling of the glucose-derived amino acids alanine and serine was not higher in cancer cells compared to PSCs in organoid co-cultures.
source: This higher M+3 level was also reflected in the other TCA cycle-derived amino acids glutamate and proline (Figure 4D–G, Figure 4—source data 1), whereas labeling of the glucose-derived amino acids alanine and serine was not higher in cancer cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Slightly higher labeling of aspartate from glutamine in protein was observed in PSCs compared to cancer cells in organoid co-cultures.
source: We also exposed organoid co-cultures to U-13C-glutamine over 4 days and traced the fate of labeled carbon into protein in each cell population. Of note, we observed slightly higher labeling of aspartate from glutamine in protein in PSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1), matching the lower fractional labeling we observed from glucose.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No appreciable differences in fractional labeling of glutamate or proline from glutamine in protein were observed between cancer cells and PSCs in organoid co-cultures.
source: We did not observe other appreciable differences in fractional labeling of glutamate or proline from glutamine in protein between cancer cells and PSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Accumulation of BFP fluorescence was slower in cancer cells compared to PSCs in 3D co-cultures, indicating that protein synthesis rates are higher in PSCs.
source: Interestingly, even though cancer cells and PSCs exhibited a similar protein synthesis rate in monoculture (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–G), accumulation of BFP fluorescence was slower in cancer cells compared to PSCs in 3D co-cultures (Figure 4H). This argues that protein synthesis rates are higher in PSCs in organoid co-cultures, and that the higher M+3 aspartate labeling observed in cancer cells cannot be explained by a higher rate of protein synthesis in the cancer cells in this co-culture system.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Significantly higher M+1 aspartate labeling in protein was observed using 1-13C-pyruvate or 3,4-13C-glucose in sorted cancer cells compared to PSCs from organoid-PSC co-cultures.
source: Compared to U-13C-glucose labeling, a greater difference and significantly higher M+1 aspartate labeling in protein was observed using 1-13C-pyruvate or 3,4-13C-glucose in sorted cancer cells compared to PSCs from organoid-PSC co-cultures, further supporting that pyruvate carboxylation activity is higher in these cells (Figure 4J–K, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J-K and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: tdTomato+ cancer cells from PDAC tumors in mice had the highest M+3 protein aspartate labeling, as well as higher M+2 aspartate labeling.
source: In agreement with labeling patterns from organoid-co-cultures, tdTomato+ cancer cells from PDAC tumors in mice had the highest M+3 protein aspartate labeling in protein, as well as higher M+2 aspartate labeling (Figure 5H–I, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H-I.

claim: Higher M+2 and M+3 labeling in glutamate but not in other glucose-labeled amino acids in protein was observed in cancer cells from PDAC tumors.
source: This labeling pattern was also reflected in higher M+2 and M+3 labeling in glutamate but not in other glucose-labeled amino acids in protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–J, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-J.

claim: PC knockdown in PDAC cells resulted in a decrease in aspartate labeling from 1-13C-pyruvate and relative pyruvate carboxylation activity compared to control cells.
source: As expected, PC knockdown in these PDAC cells resulted in a decrease in aspartate labeling from 1-13C-pyruvate and relative pyruvate carboxylation activity compared to control cells as assessed by the ratio of M+1 labeled aspartate to M+1 labeled pyruvate (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C), but did not affect proliferation in culture (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: PC knockdown in PDAC cells did not affect proliferation in culture.
source: As expected, PC knockdown in these PDAC cells resulted in a decrease in aspartate labeling from 1-13C-pyruvate and relative pyruvate carboxylation activity compared to control cells as assessed by the ratio of M+1 labeled aspartate to M+1 labeled pyruvate (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C), but did not affect proliferation in culture (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Knockdown of PC in PDAC organoids reduced growth of these cells in organoid-PSC co-cultures.
source: However, knockdown of PC in PDAC organoids reduced growth of these cells in organoid-PSC co-cultures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-G.

claim: PDAC cell lines with PC knockdown formed tumors that grew similarly to control cells when transplanted subcutaneously.
source: When transplanted subcutaneously, PDAC cell lines with PC knockdown formed tumors that grew similarly to control cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1K); however, PC expression was similar or increased in the tumors formed from PC knockdown cells compared to control tumors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1K.

claim: PC expression was similar or increased in the tumors formed from PC knockdown cells compared to control tumors.
source: When transplanted subcutaneously, PDAC cell lines with PC knockdown formed tumors that grew similarly to control cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1K); however, PC expression was similar or increased in the tumors formed from PC knockdown cells compared to control tumors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1L.

claim: Over time, cells that grew into tumors were selected for reversal of PC knockdown, suggesting that PC is required for PDAC tumor growth in vivo even though it is dispensable in culture.
source: These data suggest that over time, cells that grew into tumors were selected for reversal of PC knockdown and that PC is required for PDAC tumor growth in vivo even though it is dispensable in culture, as has been observed previously in lung cancer (Davidson et al., 2016; Fan et al., 2009; Sellers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of PC had no effect on proliferation of PDAC cells in culture.
source: Similar to knockdown experiments, loss of PC had no effect on proliferation of PDAC cells in culture (Figure 6A), whereas loss of PC reduced the growth of organoid co-cultures (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Loss of PC reduced the growth of organoid co-cultures.
source: Similar to knockdown experiments, loss of PC had no effect on proliferation of PDAC cells in culture (Figure 6A), whereas loss of PC reduced the growth of organoid co-cultures (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: PC knockout PSCs retained the ability to enhance PDAC organoid growth or growth of PDAC cancer cells as tumors in subcutaneous transplants, although the effect was reduced compared to sgControl PSCs.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 was also used to knockout PC in PSCs, and despite loss of PC expression and reduced pyruvate carboxylation activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C), PC knockout PSCs retained the ability to enhance PDAC organoid growth or growth of PDAC cancer cells as tumors in subcutaneous transplants, although the effect was reduced compared to sgControl PSCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D-F.

claim: PC-null cancer cells did not form tumors when transplanted into syngeneic mice subcutaneously or orthotopically.
source: Consistent with a requirement for PC expression in cancer cells to form PDAC tumors, PC-null cancer cells did not form tumors when transplanted into syngeneic mice subcutaneously or orthotopically (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: PC-null cancer cells still displayed M+1 aspartate labeling from 1-13C-pyruvate with similar or only a slight decrease in pyruvate carboxylation activity compared to control cells.
source: However, surprisingly, PC-null cancer cells still displayed M+1 aspartate labeling from 1-13C-pyruvate with similar or only a slight decrease in pyruvate carboxylation activity compared to control cells (Figure 6F–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Loss of PC in cancer cells can impact tumor growth, but another enzyme must also contribute to pyruvate carboxylation activity in these cells.
source: Taken together, these data argue that loss of PC in cancer cells can impact tumor growth, but another enzyme must also contribute to pyruvate carboxylation activity in these cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing residual pyruvate carboxylation activity in PC-null cells.

claim: Malic enzyme catalyzes the interconversion of pyruvate and CO2 with malate.
source: A candidate for the pyruvate carboxylation activity observed in PC-null cells is malic enzyme, since this enzyme catalyzes the interconversion of pyruvate and CO2 with malate, another 4-carbon TCA cycle intermediate.
evidence: This is based on established biochemical knowledge about malic enzyme function.

claim: Malic enzyme has been shown to be reversible and produce malate from pyruvate and CO2 in purified enzyme assays.
source: Malic enzyme is typically assumed to catalyze malate decarboxylation as a source of NADPH in cells (Cairns et al., 2011; Hosios and Vander Heiden, 2018), but has previously been shown to be reversible and produce malate from pyruvate and CO2 in purified enzyme assays (Ochoa et al., 1947; Ochoa et al., 1948).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: After knockout of both PC and ME1 in PDAC cell lines, aspartate labeling from 1-13C-pyruvate is virtually abolished.
source: After knockout of both PC and ME1 in PDAC cell lines, aspartate labeling from 1-13C-pyruvate is virtually abolished, suggesting that ME1 activity can contribute to pyruvate carboxylation activity in these cells (Figure 7A–B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Aspartate labeling was increased after exogenous expression of ME1 in PC and ME1 double knockout cells.
source: This aspartate labeling was also increased after exogenous expression of ME1 in PC and ME1 double knockout cells (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 knockout or knockdown of both PC and ME1 in organoids resulted in decreased M+1 aspartate labeling from 1-13C-pyruvate and decreased pyruvate carboxylation activity.
source: We used CRISPR/Cas9 to knockout or knockdown both PC and ME1 in organoids, which also resulted in decreased M+1 aspartate labeling from 1-13C-pyruvate and decreased pyruvate carboxylation activity (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Reduction or loss of ME1 alone in PDAC cell lines resulted in lower aspartate M+1 labeling and pyruvate carboxylation activity from 1-13C-pyruvate.
source: We also used CRISPR/Cas9 to knockout ME1 alone in PDAC cell lines and organoids (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–H). Reduction or loss of ME1 alone in PDAC cell lines resulted in lower aspartate M+1 labeling and pyruvate carboxylation activity from 1-13C-pyruvate (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–K), further suggesting a role for ME1 in anaplerosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F-K.

claim: ME1 expression in KP-/-C mouse and human PDAC tumors and organoids is more highly expressed in cancer cells compared to stroma.
source: Interestingly, ME1 expression in KP-/-C mouse and human PDAC tumors and organoids mimics that of PC in that it is more highly expressed in cancer cells compared to stroma, suggesting that ME1 could also contribute to the higher pyruvate carboxylation seen in cancer cells compared to PSCs (Figure 7C–E, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C-E and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-E.

claim: Loss of ME1 had minimal effect on cancer cell proliferation in monoculture.
source: We next assessed whether ME1 was essential for tumor and organoid growth. Similar to loss of PC, loss of ME1 had minimal effect on cancer cell proliferation in monoculture (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1F), but reduced growth of organoid co-cultures compared to controls (Figure 7G–H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Loss of ME1 reduced growth of organoid co-cultures compared to controls.
source: We next assessed whether ME1 was essential for tumor and organoid growth. Similar to loss of PC, loss of ME1 had minimal effect on cancer cell proliferation in monoculture (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1F), but reduced growth of organoid co-cultures compared to controls (Figure 7G–H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G-H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Transplantation of ME1-null cancer cells in vivo resulted in reduced tumor growth.
source: Transplantation of ME1-null cancer cells in vivo also resulted in reduced tumor growth (Figure 7I), consistent with published data (Son et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I and by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Both PC and ME1 are important enzymes for PDAC cancer cells in tumors and can contribute to the pyruvate carboxylation activity observed in pancreatic cancer.
source: Taken together, these data argue that both PC and ME1 are important enzymes for PDAC cancer cells in tumors and can contribute to the pyruvate carboxylation activity observed in pancreatic cancer.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing effects of PC and ME1 deletion on tumor growth and pyruvate carboxylation activity.

claim: Dissecting the metabolism of specific cell populations within heterogeneous systems can identify dependencies that may not be evident from studying isolated cells in culture or bulk tissue.
source: Consequently, expression of both enzymes in cancer cells was necessary for organoid and tumor growth, demonstrating that dissecting the metabolism of specific cell populations within heterogeneous systems can identify dependencies that may not be evident from studying isolated cells in culture or bulk tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: Differences in the autochthonous KP-/-C and KPC PDAC models have been attributed to differences in tumor latency and p53 status, as well as differences in how stromal cell populations interact with cancer cells to support tumor growth.
source: Despite both being driven by mutant Kras and loss of normal Trp53 function, differences in the autochthonous KP-/-C and KPC PDAC models are known and have been attributed to differences in tumor latency and p53 status, as well as differences in how stromal cell populations interact with cancer cells to support tumor growth (Rosenfeldt et al., 2013; Vennin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cell line transplantation models are thought to result in tumors with a less dense, desmoplastic stroma compared to autochthonous models.
source: To explore whether the relative abundance of cancer cells in the tumor might affect labeling, we infused mice with pancreatic tumors derived from orthotopic injection of a syngeneic KrasG12D; Trp53-/- pancreatic cancer cell line derived from tumors arising in the KP-/-C model (Danai et al., 2018), since cell line transplantation models are thought to result in tumors with a less dense, desmoplastic stroma compared to autochthonous models (Baker et al., 2016; Olive et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pancreatic stellate cells (PSCs) are a type of resident fibroblast in the pancreas which can become activated during tumorigenesis and impact the tumor microenvironment.
source: Pancreatic stellate cells (PSCs) are a type of resident fibroblast in the pancreas which can become activated during tumorigenesis and impact the tumor microenvironment (Bynigeri et al., 2017; Dunér et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PDAC tumors are FDG-PET positive.
source: Nevertheless, the findings that PDAC tumors are FDG-PET positive (Nguyen et al., 2011; Parikh et al., 2015; Yeh et al., 2018) and that levels of glucose are depleted in tumor interstitial fluid relative to plasma in PDAC mouse models (Sullivan et al., 2019), are consistent with glucose being consumed by at least some cell types within the tumor.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Levels of glucose are depleted in tumor interstitial fluid relative to plasma in PDAC mouse models.
source: Nevertheless, the findings that PDAC tumors are FDG-PET positive (Nguyen et al., 2011; Parikh et al., 2015; Yeh et al., 2018) and that levels of glucose are depleted in tumor interstitial fluid relative to plasma in PDAC mouse models (Sullivan et al., 2019), are consistent with glucose being consumed by at least some cell types within the tumor.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Utilization of ME1 to produce pyruvate from glutamine can be important for PDAC cells to maintain redox balance, specifically via NADPH generation in vitro.
source: Previous work has suggested that utilization of ME1 to produce pyruvate from glutamine can be important for PDAC cells to maintain redox balance, specifically via NADPH generation in vitro (Son et al., 2013), and that glutamine can be a major contributor to TCA metabolites in PDAC tumors (Hui et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Glutamine can be a major contributor to TCA metabolites in PDAC tumors.
source: Previous work has suggested that utilization of ME1 to produce pyruvate from glutamine can be important for PDAC cells to maintain redox balance, specifically via NADPH generation in vitro (Son et al., 2013), and that glutamine can be a major contributor to TCA metabolites in PDAC tumors (Hui et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In pancreatic β-cells, PC and ME are thought to be part of a coordinated metabolic cycle that regulates insulin secretion.
source: In pancreatic β-cells, PC and ME are thought to be part of a coordinated metabolic cycle that regulates insulin secretion (Pongratz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A dependence on pyruvate carboxylation seems to be a characteristic of both PDAC and lung tumors in vivo that is not prominent in standard cell culture systems.
source: A dependence on pyruvate carboxylation seems to be a characteristic of both PDAC and lung tumors in vivo that is not prominent in standard cell culture systems (Christen et al., 2016; Davidson et al., 2016; Fan et al., 2009; Hensley et al., 2016; Sellers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Glucose metabolism and increased glucose uptake have been shown to be important for biosynthesis in PDAC tumors.
source: Glucose metabolism and increased glucose uptake have been shown to be important for biosynthesis in PDAC tumors (Santana-Codina et al., 2018; Ying et al., 2012), but it has also been suggested that some PDAC tumors rely less on glucose for fuel and instead on alternative nutrient sources such as circulating lactate and glutamine (Hui et al., 2017), or alanine from stromal autophagy (Sousa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some PDAC tumors rely less on glucose for fuel and instead on alternative nutrient sources such as circulating lactate and glutamine, or alanine from stromal autophagy.
source: Glucose metabolism and increased glucose uptake have been shown to be important for biosynthesis in PDAC tumors (Santana-Codina et al., 2018; Ying et al., 2012), but it has also been suggested that some PDAC tumors rely less on glucose for fuel and instead on alternative nutrient sources such as circulating lactate and glutamine (Hui et al., 2017), or alanine from stromal autophagy (Sousa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Macropinocytosis to catabolize extracellular protein can be an important source of amino acids for cells in PDAC tumors.
source: For example, macropinocytosis to catabolize extracellular protein can be an important source of amino acids for cells in PDAC tumors (Commisso et al., 2013; Davidson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PDAC tumors are resistant to glutaminase inhibitors.
source: We did not see evidence for differential glutamine utilization in our organoid-PSC co-cultures, and PDAC tumors are resistant to glutaminase inhibitors (Biancur et al., 2017), but further work is needed to assess how glutamine metabolism and other anaplerotic pathways might be differentially active in cancer cells and non-cancer cells in PDAC tumors.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.
